procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated with a charge under Section 39(b) of the Army Act, 1950, related to overstaying leave.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The appellant challenged the judgment and order dated 16th February, 2015, passed by the Armed Forces Tribunal, Regional Bench, Lucknow.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant originally filed a Writ Petition before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, which was subsequently transferred to the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the dismissal of his case by the Armed Forces Tribunal, appealed to the Supreme Court.

directions: The parties are left to bear their own costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's justification for overstaying leave on the grounds of his wife's ill health was supported by sufficient evidence.

facts: The appellant claimed he overstayed his leave because his wife was seriously ill and required his presence for treatment.
He did not provide any documentary evidence, such as a treatment summary or a medical certificate, to support this claim.
The only evidence offered was his own "bald statement" during the Summary of Evidence.
The appellant also pleaded "Guilty" to the charge of overstaying his leave when it was read to him during the Summary Court Martial.
application: The Court determined that a "bald statement" without any supporting medical documentation was insufficient evidence to prove that the appellant's wife was seriously ill.
The Court also viewed the appellant's own guilty plea as a direct admission that he had overstayed his leave without a sufficient or valid reason.
The appellant's failure to provide any proof, combined with his admission of guilt, led the court to conclude that his justification was unsubstantiated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's justification for overstaying leave because he failed to provide any documentary evidence to support his claim of his wife's ill health and, furthermore, had explicitly pleaded guilty to the charge.

issue.issue_text: Whether the charge against the appellant under Section 39(b) of the Army Act, 1950, for overstaying leave, was correctly upheld by the Armed Forces Tribunal.

facts: The appellant, a Mechanical Transport Driver in the Army, was granted leave which was extended until January 15, 1999.
His subsequent request for a further extension was rejected, but he failed to rejoin his unit.
After a Court of Inquiry declared him a deserter, the appellant surrendered on May 3, 1999, having overstayed his leave by 108 days.
A Summary Court Martial (SCM) found him guilty under Section 39(b) of the Army Act and imposed the punishment of dismissal from service.
This was the appellant's sixth infraction for the same offense of overstaying leave.
The appellant's internal appeal and a subsequent petition before the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) were both dismissed.
law: Section 39(b) of the Army Act, 1950, criminalizes the act of overstaying leave without sufficient cause.
Section 71 of the Army Act lists the punishments that can be awarded by a Court Martial upon conviction. It includes imprisonment (clause c) and dismissal from service (clause e).
The Supreme Court noted that under Section 71, dismissal from service is considered a lesser punishment than imprisonment.

Regulation 448 of the Defence Service Regulations provides general instructions and a scale of punishments for SCMs, but explicitly states that it does not limit the discretion of the Court to pass any legal sentence if there is good reason.
application: The Court first dismissed the appellant's factual claim of a shorter absence, noting that he had admitted in his own statement to being absent for 108 days.

The Court rejected the appellant's argument that dismissal from service was a punishment graver than what is contemplated by the Act. It reasoned that Section 71 explicitly allows for dismissal and even classifies it as a lesser punishment than the three-year imprisonment term possible for the offense.

The Court also rejected the argument that Regulation 448 limited the SCM's power to award dismissal. It pointed out that the regulation itself preserves the SCM's discretion to impose a higher but legal punishment based on the facts of the case.

The Court found the punishment of dismissal to be justified and not disproportionate, emphasizing that this was the appellant's sixth offense of the same nature. It characterized his conduct as "gross indiscipline" that could not be tolerated in the armed forces, especially for a prolonged period of 108 days.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the Armed Forces Tribunal's decision, upholding the charge and the punishment of dismissal from service. It found no legal infirmity in the proceedings and concluded that the appellant's history of repeated offenses and the need to maintain discipline in the armed forces meant he deserved no leniency.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant's justification for overstaying leave on the grounds of his wife's ill health was supported by sufficient evidence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant made a statement during the Summary of Evidence that he had remained absent without leave on account of his wife’s ill health.
respondent_arguments: The appellant did not provide any documents, such as a treatment summary or medical certificate, to support his claim that his wife was so unwell that he needed to get her treated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the charge against the appellant under Section 39(b) of the Army Act, 1950, for overstaying leave, was correctly upheld by the Armed Forces Tribunal.
appellant_arguments: The procedure followed during the conduct of the Court of Enquiry and the Summary Court Martial (SCM) was contrary to the Rules.
respondent_arguments: The appellant pleaded guilty to the charge during the SCM and cannot be permitted to subsequently question the entire process.
The Court of Enquiry was conducted properly under the orders of the respondent No. 4, and there was no procedural error as contended by the appellant.

cases.case_name: Union of India and Others v. Ex. No. 6492086 Sep/Ash Kulbeer Singh
cases.principle: Regarding the proportionality of the punishment of dismissal from service for an offense under Section 39 of the Army Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Dismissal from service is not a disproportionate punishment for an offense that, under the governing statute, could also be punishable by imprisonment.
obiter: It is relevant to note that this was not the first occasion when the appellant had remained absent without leave. He had made a habit of remaining absent without leave even on earlier occasions.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant did not deserve any leniency or a lesser punishment because this was not his first offense; rather, it was his sixth infraction for remaining absent without leave, and he had demonstrated a failure to correct his behavior despite receiving several previous punishments ranging from fines to rigorous imprisonment.
legal_tests_applied: Proportionality of Punishment: The court assessed whether the punishment of dismissal from service was proportionate to the offense of unauthorized absence, particularly in light of the appellant's history of misconduct, referencing the precedent set in Union of India and Others v. Ex. No. 6492086 Sep/Ash Kulbeer Singh.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant was a habitual offender, as this was not the first occasion he had remained absent without leave.
This specific instance was the appellant's sixth infraction for the very same offense.
Previous, lesser punishments, including fines and rigorous imprisonment, had failed to deter the appellant's misconduct, as he 'did not mend his ways'.

Given his history as a repeat offender who was not corrected by prior punishments, the court found that he 'did not deserve any leniency by infliction of a punishment lesser than that which has been awarded to him.'
why_respondent_won: The punishment of dismissal was endorsed as being proportionate to the offense, given the appellant's extensive history of similar misconduct.
The court accepted that the appellant's repeated offenses demonstrated that lesser punishments were ineffective, justifying the more severe penalty.
The appellant's status as a six-time offender for the same charge negated any claim for leniency.
policy_considerations: The reasoning underscores the importance of discipline within the armed forces, suggesting that repeat offenses of unauthorized absence cannot be tolerated and that punishments must be sufficient to correct behavior or, failing that, to remove the offender from service.
